Qno2: What are molecular marker and its types?
A sequence of DNA or protein that can be screened to reveal key attributes of its state or composition and thus
used to reveal genetic variation it is Also known as “Genetic Marker”.

Morphological markers:

Morphological markers are those traits that are scored visually, or morphological markers are those genetic
markers whose inheritance can be followed with the naked eye.

Biochemical molecular markers

• A molecular marker is a molecule contained within a sample taken from an organism (Biochemical molecules)
• The first biochemical molecular markers used were the protein based markers.

• One of the earliest protein based markers to be used was Isozyme.

• These are different forms of an enzyme exhibiting the same catalytic activity but differing in charge and
electrophoretic mobility.

DNA based markers

• The sequence of nucleotides in DNA of an individual is unique and thus determines its identity.

• The ultimate difference between individuals lies in the nucleotide sequence of their DNA.

• These can be used to diagnose the presence of the gene without having to wait for gene effect to be seen.

Qno4: Write down the steps for the initiation and maintenance of callus
culture.

Effort by Amaan Khan

Initiation and maintenance of callus cultures

• (1) Selection of suitable parent material

• (2) Choice of explant and method of isolation

• (3) Culture medium and conditions required

• (4) Optimization of culture conditions

Selection of suitable parent material

• Parent plant must be healthy and free from decay or disease

• Mother plant be actively growing and not be about to enter a period of dormancy

Choice of explant and method of isolation

• Any part of mother plant; Plant organs or specific plant tissue or plant cells

• Explant must contain living cells

• Younger tissue is more callus responsive due to the presence of large no. of actively dividing cells

• Explants isolated in sterile conditions

• Ensure proper sterilization methods for a particular explants

Culture medium and conditions required

• Culture the sterilized explants on suitable autoclaved culture medium

• Incubate cultures at 22-24 ± 2°C in light or dark

• Most callus will be initiated from the cut surfaces within 3-8 wks.

Optimization of culture conditions

• Consult literature to know previous callus initiation attempts for species under consideration

• For pioneering callus culture attempt, modify medium previously used for a related species

• Start with one of the defined media and manipulate hormone concentrations

• Set up a growth Latin Square of 25 culture plates with 5 each of auxin and cytokinin conc.

• Callus for this growth trial should be uniform and of large (20 mg) size.

A herbicide’s effectiveness is strongly influenced by its toxic mode of action and the application method. Herbicides
can act by inhibiting a plant’s amino acid production, growth, photosynthesis, cell division, or by mimicking natural

Qno11: What are Somaclonal variations?                                    3 marks

Somaclonal Variation

• In addition to the variants/mutants (cell lines and plants) obtained as a result of the application of a selective agent
in the presence or absence of a mutagen, many variants have been obtained through the tissue culture cycle itself.

• These somaclonal variants, which are dependent on the natural variation in a population of cells, may be genetic or
epigenetic, and are usually observed in the regenerated plantlets.

Agrobacterium-Mediated Gene Transfer in Plants: Mechanism, Effectiveness, and a Real-
World Success Story

Introduction

Gene transfer technologies have revolutionized plant biotechnology by enabling the development
of genetically modified crops with enhanced traits. Among these, the Agrobacterium
tumefaciens-mediated gene transfer method has become a cornerstone technique due to its
specificity, stability, and integration capabilities (Gelvin, 2017). This natural plant pathogen has
been harnessed to introduce desired genes into plant genomes, offering a reliable tool for both
basic research and crop improvement.

Mechanism of Agrobacterium-Mediated Gene Transfer

Agrobacterium tumefaciens naturally transfers part of its DNA (the T-DNA) from the tumor-
inducing (Ti) plasmid into the plant genome. This process involves several coordinated steps:

   1. Recognition and Attachment: The bacterium identifies wounded plant cells and attaches
      to their surfaces through virulence (vir) genes.
   2. T-DNA Processing and Transfer: The T-DNA is excised from the plasmid and
      transferred into the plant cell through a type IV secretion system (Gelvin, 2010).
   3. Integration into Plant Genome: Once inside, the T-DNA integrates into the plant's
      nuclear DNA, leading to stable genetic transformation.

This method has been optimized to deliver foreign genes by replacing tumor-inducing genes with
beneficial transgenes, turning Agrobacterium into a genetic engineering tool rather than a
pathogen (Hwang et al., 2018).

Effectiveness of the Method

Agrobacterium-mediated transformation is notably effective for several reasons:

   •   High Stability: The T-DNA integrates into the host genome in a relatively stable and
       predictable manner.
   •   Low Copy Number: It typically results in the insertion of one or a few copies of the
       gene, minimizing gene silencing issues (Sharma et al., 2020).

   •   Targeted Transformation: This technique tends to favor transformation in nuclear
       regions conducive to gene expression.
   •   Reduced Gene Rearrangement: Compared to other methods like particle bombardment,
       it causes fewer rearrangements or mutations during gene insertion.

These features make Agrobacterium-based transformation especially suitable for dicotyledonous
plants, though significant advancements have allowed successful applications in monocots as
well.

Advantages Over Other Gene Transfer Methods

Compared to direct gene transfer techniques such as biolistics or electroporation, Agrobacterium-
mediated transformation offers multiple advantages:

   •   Cost-Effectiveness: The process requires relatively simple lab infrastructure.
   •   Natural Mechanism: Since the bacterium uses a natural infection process, it is less
       invasive than physical or chemical methods.
   •   Efficient Selection: Transgenic lines developed via this method exhibit high
       transformation efficiency with lower somaclonal variation (Hiei et al., 2014).
   •   Suitability for Complex Traits: It is well-suited for introducing multigene constructs
       due to its stable gene expression profile.

These attributes have led to its widespread use in academic research and commercial crop
development.

Real-World Example: Agrobacterium-Mediated Transformation of Bt Cotton

A well-documented success story of Agrobacterium-mediated transformation is the development
of Bt cotton—a genetically modified variety engineered to express Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)
toxin, which is lethal to bollworms and other insect pests.

Background

India, among other countries, faced severe cotton yield losses due to Helicoverpa armigera
infestations. Traditional pesticides proved inadequate, leading to environmental and health
concerns. Genetic modification using Bt genes provided an effective alternative.

Transformation Process

The Bt gene (Cry1Ac) was inserted into cotton cells using Agrobacterium tumefaciens. The
transformed cells were cultured, selected using marker genes, and regenerated into full plants

(Kranthi, 2011). This method ensured stable integration and consistent expression of the Bt toxin
in plant tissues.

Impact and Success

Since its commercialization in 2002, Bt cotton has transformed Indian agriculture:

   •   Pest Resistance: Yield losses due to bollworms dropped significantly.
   •   Increased Yield: Average yields rose by 30–40% in regions adopting Bt cotton (Qaim &
       Zilberman, 2003).
   •   Reduced Pesticide Use: Farmers reported a 50–60% reduction in insecticide application.
   •   Economic Benefits: Net profits per hectare increased, improving livelihoods in rural
       communities.

The use of Agrobacterium-mediated transformation was pivotal in achieving a stable, long-
lasting expression of the Bt gene, which helped sustain cotton production with minimal
environmental damage (James, 2010).

Limitations and Considerations

Despite its advantages, some challenges remain:

   •   Host Range Limitation: Initially, Agrobacterium was ineffective in many monocots like
       wheat and maize. However, modern super-binary vectors and modified strains have
       expanded its utility.
   •   Regulatory and Public Concerns: Like all GM crops, those developed through
       Agrobacterium transformation face biosafety and labeling regulations.
   •   Tissue Culture Dependency: The technique still requires sophisticated tissue culture
       steps, which may limit its accessibility in resource-constrained settings (Altpeter et al.,
       2016).

Addressing these issues continues to be a focus in plant biotechnology research.

Cell Culture and Crop Improvement: Exploring the Frontier of Agricultural
Biotechnology

1. Introduction: Cell Culture in Agriculture

Cell culture is a key instrument in the toolbox of agricultural biotechnology, allowing scientists to
grow and manipulate plant cells in controlled environments. This innovative technology offers
precise, efficient, and scalable means to improve crop varieties in ways that traditional plant
breeding methods cannot achieve.

2. Accelerating Plant Breeding with Protoplast Fusion

Cell culture enables protoplast fusion, which is the fusion of plant cells stripped of their cell walls,
permitting genetic material exchange from different plant species. This method allows breeders to
introduce novel traits into crops, including disease resistance or drought tolerance, accelerating the
process of creating superior crop varieties.

3. Developing Transgenic Crops via Agrobacterium-Mediated Transformation

Cell culture has paved the way for Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, a revolutionary
method to genetically engineer plants. By introducing desired genes into the plant cells, this
technique enables the production of transgenic crops with enhanced traits such as pest resistance,
nutritional content, and yield.

4. Empowering Crop Conservation with Cryopreservation

Cryopreservation of plant cell cultures ensures the conservation of valuable crop genetic resources.
By freezing cells at extremely low temperatures, the genetic material can be stored indefinitely,
safeguarding biodiversity and providing a reservoir of genetic material for future crop
improvement efforts.

5. Harnessing Somatic Embryogenesis for Mass Propagation

Somatic embryogenesis, the process where a plant embryo is developed from somatic (non-
reproductive) cells, has vast implications for mass propagation of high-yielding or disease-resistant
crop varieties. This process allows for large-scale, cost-effective production of genetically identical
plants.

6. Exploiting Haploid and Doubled Haploid Production for Breeding

Cell culture enables the creation of haploid and doubled haploid plants, containing a single set of
chromosomes. Such plants can speed up breeding programs, because they allow for homozygous
lines to be developed in a single generation, vastly accelerating the breeding process.

7. Enhancing Crop Resistance through Somaclonal Variation

Cell culture can generate somaclonal variation, which is the genetic variation arising from the
propagation of tissue culture. This source of variation can be harnessed to develop crop varieties
with improved resistance to diseases, pests, and environmental stresses.

8. Transforming Secondary Metabolite Production with Cell Suspension
Cultures

Cell suspension cultures offer a scalable and controlled method for the production of valuable
secondary metabolites, such as flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenoids, which have diverse uses
ranging from pharmaceuticals to biofuels. This technology holds promise for enhancing the
economic viability of many crops.

9. Enabling Functional Genomics and Proteomics Research

Cell culture is an essential tool for functional genomics and proteomics studies in crops. It allows
researchers to understand gene function and protein interactions, providing critical insights into
plant development, disease resistance, and stress tolerance mechanisms.

10. Conclusion: Shaping the Future of Agriculture with Cell Culture

As we face global challenges, such as population growth, climate change, and food security, cell
culture stands as a powerful ally in crop improvement. This technology, by enabling precise,
scalable, and innovative crop modifications, is bound to shape the future of agriculture, driving us
towards a more sustainable and secure global food system.

3. Developing Transgenic Crops via Agrobacterium-Mediated Transformation

Cell culture has paved the way for Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, a revolutionary
method to genetically engineer plants. By introducing desired genes into the plant cells, this
technique enables the production of transgenic crops with enhanced traits such as pest resistance,
nutritional content, and yield.

4. Empowering Crop Conservation with Cryopreservation

Cryopreservation of plant cell cultures ensures the conservation of valuable crop genetic resources.
By freezing cells at extremely low temperatures, the genetic material can be stored indefinitely,
safeguarding biodiversity and providing a reservoir of genetic material for future crop
improvement efforts.

5. Harnessing Somatic Embryogenesis for Mass Propagation

Somatic embryogenesis, the process where a plant embryo is developed from somatic (non-
reproductive) cells, has vast implications for mass propagation of high-yielding or disease-resistant
crop varieties. This process allows for large-scale, cost-effective production of genetically identical
plants.

6. Exploiting Haploid and Doubled Haploid Production for Breeding

Cell culture enables the creation of haploid and doubled haploid plants, containing a single set of
chromosomes. Such plants can speed up breeding programs, because they allow for homozygous
lines to be developed in a single generation, vastly accelerating the breeding process.

7. Enhancing Crop Resistance through Somaclonal Variation

Cell culture can generate somaclonal variation, which is the genetic variation arising from the
propagation of tissue culture. This source of variation can be harnessed to develop crop varieties
with improved resistance to diseases, pests, and environmental stresses.

8. Transforming Secondary Metabolite Production with Cell Suspension
Cultures

Cell suspension cultures offer a scalable and controlled method for the production of valuable
secondary metabolites, such as flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenoids, which have diverse uses
ranging from pharmaceuticals to biofuels. This technology holds promise for enhancing the
economic viability of many crops.

9. Enabling Functional Genomics and Proteomics Research

Cell culture is an essential tool for functional genomics and proteomics studies in crops. It allows
researchers to understand gene function and protein interactions, providing critical insights into
plant development, disease resistance, and stress tolerance mechanisms.

10. Conclusion: Shaping the Future of Agriculture with Cell Culture

As we face global challenges, such as population growth, climate change, and food security, cell
culture stands as a powerful ally in crop improvement. This technology, by enabling precise,
scalable, and innovative crop modifications, is bound to shape the future of agriculture, driving us
towards a more sustainable and secure global food system.

Agriculture Biotechnology is collection of scientific techniques to improve plants,
animals and microorganisms, to manipulate the genetic makeup, for the production or
processing of agricultural products, to Increase agricultural productivity, to enhance
breeders’ ability to make improvements in crops and livestock and to enable
improvements that are not possible with traditional crossing of related species alone.

5 Transform Process with example and how transform plants?

Bacteria can take up foreign DNA in a process called transformation. Transformation is
a key step in DNA cloning. Plastids, particularly chloroplasts, are used for
transformation in plants because they contain their own DNA and can be genetically
modified to express desired traits. This allows for targeted modifications in
photosynthesis, metabolic pathways, and other important cellular functions.

7 Germplasm preservation:

Germplasm is living tissue from which new plants can be grown. It can be a seed or
another plant part a leaf, a piece of stem, pollen or even just a few cells that can be
turned into a whole plant. Germplasm preservation refers to the collection, storage, and
maintenance of plant or animal genetic resources to ensure their long-term availability
for future use in breeding, research, and conservation purposes.

8 What is crown mady disease:

 Crown gall disease, also known as crown mady disease, is a plant disease caused by
the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens. It leads to the formation of tumor-like
growths on the crown and roots of infected plants, negatively impacting their growth and
productivity.

1= A herbicide’s effectiveness is strongly influenced by its toxic mode of action and the
application method.

2= Herbicides can act by inhibiting a plant’s amino acid production, growth,
photosynthesis, cell division, or by mimicking natural auxin hormones to cause
deformities.

 3= Most modern herbicides are synthetic mimics of a natural plant’s hormones that
obstruct the target plant’s growth. Some plants such as the tree of heaven and juglans
(walnuts) produce their own natural herbicide.

 4= Organic herbicides are useful and are commonly used in organic gardens, but they
are less effective and more costly than synthetic herbicides because they based on
natural materials.

 Several colonies are checked to identify one with the right plasmid (e.g., by PCR or
restriction digest).The bacteria that make colonies should all contain a plasmid (which
provides antibiotic resistance). However, it’s not necessarily the case that all of the
plasmid-containing colonies will have the same plasmid.

11 Symptoms of peripheral neuropathy:

 Symptoms of peripheral neuropathy can include numbness, tingling, pain, weakness,
loss of coordination, and sensitivity to touch or temperature changes in the affected
areas.

13 Role of auxin in plants:

Auxin plays a crucial role in plants, promoting cell elongation, root development, apical
dominance, tropic responses, and differentiation of vascular tissues, as well as
influencing fruit development and abscission.

 Suitable alternative to traditional methods

 Ease in keeping, packing and transport of material multiplied by micropropagation.

15 Direct Organogenesis

The production of direct buds or shoots from a tissue with no intervening callus stage is
termed direct organogenesis. Plants have been propagated by direct organogenesis for
improved multiplication rates, production of transgenic plants, and—most importantly—
for clonal propagation. Typically, indirect organogenesis is more important for
transgenic plant production.

Plastids are the major organelle of plant and algal cells. These are the site of
manufacture and storage of important chemical compounds. It has circular, dsDNA
copies and it replicates autonomously of the cell. Plastids are thought to have been
originated from endosymbiotic bacteria and plastid genes show maternal inheritance.

 What are molecular markers?5
• Scientists can use molecular markers to select plants or animals that
possess a desirable gene, even in the absence of a visible trait.
• Thus, breeding is more precise and efficient.
Types of Molecular markers
Morphological markers:
• Morphological markers are those traits
that are scored visually, or
morphological markers are those
genetic markers whose inheritance can
be followed with the naked eye.
• A molecular marker is a molecule contained within a sample taken
from an organism (Biochemical molecules)
• The first biochemical molecular markers used were the protein based
markers.
• One of the earliest protein based markers to be used was Isozyme.
• These are different forms of an enzyme exhibiting the same catalytic
activity but differing in charge and electrophoretic mobility.
DNA based markers
• The sequence of nucleotides in DNA of an individual is unique and
thus determines its identity.
• The ultimate difference between individuals lies in the nucleotide
sequence of their DNA.
• These can be used to diagnose the presence of the gene without having
to wait for gene effect to be seen.
